To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the effect of the different multiple primary rules on survival estimates depends on the cancer site, and that using all first cancers (SEER or International Association of Cancer Registry rules) to produce survival estimates results in less biased estimates than using first cancers-only.

the use of SEER or IACRs multiple primary rules for identifying primary cancers did not affect the survival estimates of all cancers matching the selection criterion, but did affect the survival estimates for first primary cancers-only.

(1) the percentage of multiple primary (MP; all sites combined) cancers increased 25.1 % (SEER rules) and 19.9 % (IACR rules) among men and 24.8 % (SEer rules) and 20.3 % (IARC rules) among women; (2) the percentage of MP cancer was higher among females than among men, and the difference was larger by using SEER than IARC rules
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of multiple primary cancer rules on cancer survival estimates and the effect of multiple cancers on survival.
the effect of multiple primary (MP)-cancer registration rules on cancer survival.
the effect of multiple primary cancer rules (SEER and IACRA) on survival estimates for cancer patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
SEER and IARC rules are not interchangeable and should not be used interchangeably.
SEER estimates are similar to IACR survival estimates, and both are comparable to estimates restricted to first cancers-only, if all first cancers are included in the analysis.
SEER and IARC rules do not affect survival rates if all first cancers are used to calculate the survival rates.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
SEER and IARC rules do not significantly impact survival rates, but SEER rules are more inclusive than IACR.

cancer patients remain at high risk of subsequent cancers and that survival estimates should not be restricted to first primary cases only, but should instead include all cancers matching the selection criterion.
cancer registries should use a common set of rules for identifying primary cancers, and that survival estimates should be based on all first cancers matching a common set of selection criteria.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cancer registries and researchers should not exclude MP cancers from analyses of cancer survival.
the use of first cancers-only in cancer survival analyses is no longer appropriate and that the use of SEER or IACRs MP rules to identify first cancers is not necessary.
the multiple primary rules used to identify primary cases do not affect the survival estimates if all cancers matching the selection criterion are used to produce the estimates.
